name: Stimulant use disorder
summary: No medication is FDA-approved for cocaine or methamphetamine/amphetamine-type stimulant use disorder. Contingency management is the evidence-based standard. The 2024 ASAM/AAAP guideline lists several off-label medications as conditional options with low-to-moderate certainty evidence; psychostimulant prescribing is restricted to addiction specialists with close monitoring.
plainSummary: Stimulant use disorder involves trouble controlling use of drugs like methamphetamine or cocaine. No medicine is approved for it yet, but counseling programs that reward drug-free tests work well, and some medicines may help.
noApprovedNote: No FDA-approved medication exists for stimulant (cocaine, methamphetamine, or other amphetamine-type) use disorder as of October 2026. Searches of FDA announcements for 2024–2026 found no approvals. Contingency management, a behavioral treatment, is the best-supported intervention. All medications below are off-label.

offLabel.use: Reduce methamphetamine use (amphetamine-type stimulant use disorder)
offLabel.notes: In ADAPT-2 (NEJM 2021), XR-naltrexone 380 mg every 3 weeks plus bupropion XL 450 mg/day produced a modest but significant increase in response (methamphetamine-negative urines) versus placebo. ASAM/AAAP 2024 gives it a conditional recommendation (moderate certainty). Cautions: patients must be opioid-free, bupropion lowers the seizure threshold, and naltrexone causes injection-site reactions. Cost and access are barriers.

details.labeledFor: Naltrexone XR is FDA-approved for alcohol and opioid dependence; bupropion XL for depression and SAD prevention. The combination is not labeled for methamphetamine use disorder.

dosing.start: Bupropion XL titrated up to 450 mg/day; naltrexone XR 380 mg IM
dosing.target: Naltrexone XR 380 mg IM every 3 weeks plus bupropion XL 450 mg daily (ADAPT-2)
dosing.max: Bupropion XL 450 mg/day; naltrexone XR labeled interval is every 4 weeks
dosing.notes: Patients must be opioid-free for 7–10 days.

boxedWarnings: Suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, adolescents, and young adults
contraindications: Naltrexone: current opioid use, acute opioid withdrawal, positive opioid screen
Bupropion: seizure disorder, bulimia/anorexia, abrupt alcohol or sedative withdrawal, MAOI use
warnings: Precipitated opioid withdrawal; loss of opioid tolerance and overdose risk
details.plainSummary: A monthly-style injection plus a daily pill modestly increased methamphetamine-free urine tests in a large trial. Cost and access are limits.

references.label: Trivedi MH, et al. Bupropion and naltrexone in methamphetamine use disorder. N Engl J Med 2021
ASAM/AAAP Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Stimulant Use Disorder. J Addict Med 2024

offLabel.notes: Coffin 2020 showed reduced methamphetamine use at 30 mg/day among men and transgender women who have sex with men. A 2026 Australian phase 3 trial reported a modest reduction in use days. ASAM/AAAP 2024: conditional, low certainty. Cautions: sedation, weight gain, and antidepressant suicidality warning.

details.labeledFor: FDA-approved for major depressive disorder; not for methamphetamine use disorder.

dosing.notes: Used in men and transgender women who have sex with men in the key trial.

boxedWarnings: Suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, adolescents, and young adults
details.plainSummary: An antidepressant that cut methamphetamine use in one trial, with sleepiness and weight gain as side effects.

references.label: Coffin PO, et al. Effects of mirtazapine for methamphetamine use disorder. JAMA Psychiatry 2020
ASAM/AAAP Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Stimulant Use Disorder. J Addict Med 2024

offLabel.use: Reduce cocaine use; also considered for amphetamine-type stimulant use
offLabel.notes: Johnson 2013 found more cocaine-free weeks with topiramate titrated to 300 mg/day. ASAM/AAAP 2024 gives conditional, low-certainty recommendations for cocaine use disorder (especially with co-occurring AUD) and for ATS use disorder. Cautions: cognitive slowing, paresthesia, kidney stones, metabolic acidosis, and teratogenicity.

details.labeledFor: FDA-approved for epilepsy and migraine prevention; not for cocaine or amphetamine use disorders.

dosing.notes: Slow titration; conditional, low-certainty guideline support.

details.plainSummary: An epilepsy medicine that increased cocaine-free weeks in a trial, particularly when drinking is also a problem.

references.label: Johnson BA, et al. Topiramate for the treatment of cocaine addiction: a randomized clinical trial. JAMA Psychiatry 2013
ASAM/AAAP Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Stimulant Use Disorder. J Addict Med 2024

offLabel.use: Promote cocaine abstinence; reduce methamphetamine use in lower-frequency users (<18 days/month)
offLabel.notes: ASAM/AAAP 2024 gives conditional, low-certainty recommendations, with extra consideration when tobacco use disorder or depression co-occurs. Benefit as monotherapy is modest and inconsistent. Cautions: seizure risk (avoid with eating disorders or seizure history) and insomnia.

details.labeledFor: FDA-approved for depression, SAD prevention, and smoking cessation; not for stimulant use disorders.

dosing.target: 300 mg/day (up to 450 mg/day in combination protocols)
dosing.notes: Modest and inconsistent benefit as a single drug.

boxedWarnings: Suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, adolescents, and young adults
details.plainSummary: Bupropion may help some people cut down on cocaine or lighter methamphetamine use, especially if they also smoke or are depressed.

references.label: ASAM/AAAP Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Stimulant Use Disorder. J Addict Med 2024

offLabel.agent: Prescription psychostimulants (extended-release amphetamine salts, long-acting methylphenidate, modafinil)
offLabel.use: Agonist-type treatment: long-acting amphetamine or modafinil for cocaine use disorder (also topiramate + ER mixed amphetamine salts); long-acting methylphenidate for ATS use disorder
offLabel.notes: ASAM/AAAP 2024 gives conditional recommendations (low to moderate certainty) but limits them to board-certified addiction specialists or equivalently trained physicians able to monitor closely (pill counts, drug testing, PDMP checks). Some regimens used doses at or above ADHD maximums. Cautions: misuse and diversion, cardiovascular effects, psychosis, and Schedule II/IV prescribing rules.

details.labeledFor: These stimulants are FDA-approved for ADHD and narcolepsy (modafinil for sleepiness disorders); none is approved for stimulant use disorders.

dosing.start: Start at standard ADHD starting doses
dosing.target: Cocaine: ER mixed amphetamine salts 60–80 mg/day or modafinil 200–400 mg/day; ATS: long-acting methylphenidate (some studies up to 180 mg/day)
dosing.max: Some regimens exceed ADHD maximums; limit to addiction specialists
dosing.notes: Pill counts, urine testing, and PDMP checks are expected.

details.plainSummary: Prescription stimulants are sometimes used as a substitute treatment for stimulant addiction, but only by trained addiction specialists with close monitoring.

references.label: ASAM/AAAP Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Stimulant Use Disorder. J Addict Med 2024
